title: Homeless by Choice
dek: You're 23, no car, no loans, a job you hate. Seattle will feed you, wash you, insure you and, if you get in, house you for free. We ran the numbers on quitting. Here's the bill.
body: Every Seattle office worker has had the thought. You're on the bus at 7:40 a.m., your rent just went up again, and some guy stretched out in a doorway on Third looks like he's winning. What if he's the smart one?

So let's take the thought seriously. Picture a 23-year-old who never went to college, owes nobody, drives nothing, and spends 40 hours a week at a job that's slowly eating them. Could they just walk away and live on what this city gives out for free?
The answer is more interesting than either side wants it to be.
## Breakfast is handled

Start in Ballard. Edible Hope Kitchen serves a free breakfast every weekday from 8 to 10 in the basement of St. Paul's United Church of Christ, on 12th Ave NW. Friday is pancakes and eggs. Other days it's curry, meatloaf, sometimes salmon. No sign-up, no sermon, no bill.

Down the hill, the Ballard Food Bank hands out groceries and bags built for people with no stove, and runs a Kindness Café Monday through Thursday. Sunday night there's a free dinner at Ballard First Lutheran. On Capitol Hill, Community Lunch serves weekday breakfast and lunch to anyone who walks in, plus coats, socks and sleeping bags.

Showers and laundry? Urban Rest Stop does both, free, with towels, soap and detergent thrown in. Internet? The Seattle Public Library gives you free Wi-Fi whenever it’s open and two hours a day on a computer with a card. A church on a Sunday morning, if that's your thing.
None of this is one place that does everything. It's a patchwork with opening hours. But stitched together, it covers a surprising amount of a normal life.

Programs change; check before you go."}
## The roof is the hard part

Free shelter exists, and some of it is better than you'd think. SHARE/WHEEL's Tent City 3 and Tent City 4 charge nothing, have no set limit on how long you can stay, and run themselves: residents set the rules, pull security shifts, and get hot dinners from volunteers most nights, plus bus tickets.

A step up is a tiny-house village. The Low Income Housing Institute's units have a locking door, a bed, heat, electricity and storage, with shared kitchens and bathrooms. Nickelsville runs self-managed villages too. Listings say no fees.

Here's the catch nobody puts on the brochure: you have to get in. LIHI takes referrals through outreach workers and requires case management. Nickelsville runs interviews and a waitlist. And the demand is enormous. King County counted 18,365 people experiencing homelessness this year, 11,829 of them without shelter, up 9 percent from 2024.

Then there's the park. Rent there is zero too, but camping in Seattle parks is generally illegal. You get no lock, no heat, no neighbors watching your stuff, and no guarantee you'll be allowed to stay the night.
So, three places with the same rent, $0, and wildly different lives. That's the whole story in one line.
## Run the receipts

Here's the math, honestly. Two workers paying normal Seattle costs: one living alone, one splitting a place. Then our dropout, assuming they've already landed a free bed, signed up for benefits and eat from the free network. No car anywhere. No debt anywhere.

The roommate rent and small items are our assumptions. Transit is a full-price Metro pass, or a $36 ORCA LIFT pass for low-income riders. The third column only works if every condition is met."}
Thirty-six dollars a month. That number is real, and it's why the thought won't go away.

But look at what it's hiding. The worker paying $2,042 a month is also earning. Give our roommate an illustrative $3,200 a month after tax and they clear about $1,158 after bills. Our dropout clears nothing, because there's nothing coming in. Skipping rent isn't the same as saving money. You've traded a paycheck for your time. For some people that's a great trade. It's still a trade.
And the worker could cheat too. Housed people can eat at Community Lunch and use the library. Push the roommate onto the same free network and their bill drops to about $1,466 a month.
## The paper route

There's a third option the shouting match usually misses: no rent, and a little income. Real Change vendors buy each paper for $1.25 and sell it for $4, plus tips. That's $2.75 a copy, and you set your own hours, with no boss and no performance review.

Before tips, taxes, bus fare and unsold copies. Not a promise of what anyone earns."}

Sell 200 papers and you've got about $500 a month of walking-around money on a $0 rent bill. On paper, that's the most livable version of the whole plan. Whether you can actually sell 200 papers a month, nobody publishes.
## The free stuff has strings
The benefits are real. They're also not forever, and they're not automatic.

Washington's food stamps, called Basic Food, max out at $306 a month for one person. But able-bodied adults without kids now face time limits statewide unless they work or train about 80 hours a month, or put in Workfare hours. Quit a job without good cause and you can be sanctioned too. "Quit and live on EBT forever" isn't how the rules work.

Health care is the big one. Apple Health covers doctors and mental health for eligible low-income adults at no cost to you, which kills the old argument that you have to stay at a job you hate for the insurance. But starting January 2027, the state says many adults on Apple Health will face new work or community-service requirements and renewals every six months. The free ride has a clock on it.
## What it does to you

Your body notices where you sleep. A heated tiny house and a wet sidewalk are not the same life with the same rent. A national study tracking about 140,000 people counted as homeless in the 2010 Census found that those under 65 died at roughly three and a half times the rate of housed people. That's a broad population, not a prediction about one healthy 23-year-old in a village. But it's not nothing.

The office isn't a spa either. The World Health Organization says decent work gives people purpose, routine and connection, and that bad work with crushing demands, bullying and no control wrecks mental health. If your job is the second kind, wanting out is sane.

Just know that the free life has a schedule too. Breakfast ends at 10. Laundry runs about an hour and a half a load. Camps have chores and meetings. You trade a boss for a calendar of serving windows.
## The part money can't measure
The best case for this life isn't financial. It's people.

In a 2023 podcast recorded inside Tent City 3, one resident called the camp "the family that I got to pick." Researchers who studied the camp from 2012 to 2025 found that its shared chores and resident-run rules gave people real connection and a sense of control. Showing up for a security shift, sharing dinner, being trusted by your neighbors: that's a kind of worth no paycheck hands out.
Of course you don't have to be homeless to have any of that. Housed people volunteer, worship and build community too, if their jobs leave them the energy.
## So, is it a career?

As a way to live on almost no cash, yes, under the right conditions: you're healthy, you get into a good village, your benefits hold, and you keep a little income on the side. Seattle really has built a city where the basics can cost zero.

As a plan, it's shakier. Beds are scarce, rules are tightening, and the safety net gets thinner the moment you lean on it hardest. Walk out of your apartment assuming a tiny house is waiting and you may find a waitlist and a park.

And calling it "homeless by choice" lumps together people who got evicted, people who turned down a bad shelter, people who love their camp and people who just can't do another year of a soul-killing job. Those aren't the same decision.

Here's what the numbers really show. Strip away rent and the basics of a life cost almost nothing in this city. What costs so much is the roof. If the best deal a 23-year-old can find is a job whose main reward is being allowed to stay indoors, that says less about the 23-year-old than it does about Seattle.
